parts.text:
The user wants to set up a new Rust project for a systems tool that needs to call native C library functions and use OS-level C types directly. This implies FFI (Foreign Function Interface) with C, likely using the `libc` crate and `bindgen` for generating bindings, and perhaps `cc` crate for building C code.

Let me check the opencode.json and .opencode for context.

The user wants a new Rust project. Let me set it up. It's a fresh empty git repo. I should create a Cargo project with appropriate dependencies for FFI: `libc` and `bindgen` (build dependency), possibly `cc`.

Let me plan:
1. `cargo init --name <name>` - need a project name. The user didn't give one. I'll pick something sensible like `sys-tool`. Actually let me not overthink. Let me create in current directory since /work is the workspace. But `cargo init` in /work will create src/main.rs and Cargo.toml.

Let me consider whether to ask for a name. The instruction is to set up a new project. I'll pick a reasonable name. Maybe ask? Better to just do it. But naming matters. I'll use `sys-tool`.

Let me use `cargo init` since directory has files already (git repo). `cargo init` works in existing dir.

Dependencies for calling native C functions and OS-level C types:
- `libc` crate for OS C types.
- `bindgen` as build-dependency to generate bindings.
- `cc` as build-dependency to compile any bundled C code.

I'll set up the project structure with a build.rs using bindgen, a wrapper.h, and maybe an example C library. Actually the user said "needs to call native C library functions" — could be system libc functions. bindgen setup is good for that.

Let me create a solid scaffold. Let me first init.
I'll scaffold a Rust project configured for C FFI. Let me initialize it first.

No clang, no llvm-config. bindgen requires libclang. So if I add bindgen as a build-dependency, the build will fail. I should either not include bindgen or note it. Hmm.

The user wants to call native C library functions and use OS-level C types. The core dependency is `libc`. For calling system functions, `libc` crate with `extern "C"` declarations is the standard approach. bindgen is optional for generating bindings to custom headers, but requires libclang at build time.

Let me check if cc/gcc is available for the cc crate.

parts.text:
All clean. Let me summarize the setup concisely.

Project structure:
- Cargo.toml: libc dep, cc build-dep
- build.rs: compiles src/native/example.c
- src/native/example.c: native C library
- src/ffi.rs: unsafe extern "C" bindings + safe wrappers, uses libc types
- src/main.rs: usage

I should mention bindgen is the usual next step if they have libclang, since they may want to generate bindings for larger headers. Keep concise.

Done. Working FFI scaffold at `/work`:

- `Cargo.toml` — `libc` (OS C types) + `cc` (build-dep)
- `build.rs:1` — compiles `src/native/example.c` into a static lib
- `src/native/example.c` — native C functions using `size_t`/`off_t`/`pid_t`
- `src/ffi.rs:8` — `unsafe extern "C"` block plus safe wrappers; `#[repr(C)]` struct
- `src/main.rs` — calls the C lib and `libc::getpid` directly

`cargo run`, `fmt`, and `clippy` all pass clean.

For large C headers, add `bindgen` in `build.rs` to auto-generate bindings — note it requires `libclang` (not installed here).
